title: Be a renunciant at home
hook: re man aiso kar sanniaasaa: make your home your forest, your heart your hermitage (Dasam, Ramkali Patshahi 10)

segments.voice: Yesterday, grant me this, and your line: never turn from good. Did you do the good deed you chose, even when the moment to back out came? Today, the Tenth Guru again, this time on where a spiritual life is lived. Day six hundred seventy-three.

It's an old fantasy: quit the job, sell the stuff, move to a cabin in the mountains, and finally become the calm, deep person ordinary life never leaves time for. In India, that dream has an old and honored form: the sannyasi, the renunciant who leaves home for the forest, with matted hair and ashes on the skin. Guru Gobind Singh wrote a shabad that takes every piece of that picture, one by one, and moves it indoors. Today: be a renunciant at home.
screen: `THE CABIN IN THE MOUNTAINS.` → `THE SANNYASI IN THE FOREST.` → `EVERY PIECE MOVED INDOORS.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Raag Ramkali, among the Tenth Guru's hymns in the Dasam Granth. It opens: re man aiso kar sanniaasaa. In paraphrase: O mind, practice renunciation like this. Think of your whole house as the forest, and stay detached inside your own heart. Then it goes through the renunciant's kit, item by item, and gives each one a new meaning. Make self-control your matted hair. Make union with God your daily bath. Let your teacher be wisdom, and smear the Name on yourself like ashes. Eat little, sleep little, love mercy and forgiveness. Keep a gentle, contented nature, and keep lust, anger, pride, greed and attachment out of the mind. It's a clever move. The shabad doesn't mock the renunciant. It takes the forest life seriously, and then says the real forest is a way of living, and you can carry it into a kitchen. That's a deep thread in Sikh teaching, running back to Guru Nanak, who lived as a householder and taught that God is found in the middle of ordinary life, not by escaping it. The word for the inner detachment here is udaas: unattached, free inside. You can be udaas in a crowded house, and caught in a quiet cave. So the question isn't where you live. It's whether, in the middle of the noise, there's a small clearing inside you where the Name is remembered.
screen: `O MIND, RENOUNCE LIKE THIS.` · `YOUR HOUSE IS THE FOREST.` · `THE KIT, GIVEN NEW MEANING.` · `A CLEARING IN A FULL HOUSE.` · then, large: `THE FOREST AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make your room a hermitage for a minute. Stay exactly where you are; don't tidy anything. Let the room be the forest. Notice its sounds as if they were birds and wind: the fridge, traffic, someone in the next room. Sit as still as a hermit would. Feel your feet as rooted. If you pray, you can say Waheguru in the clearing you've made. The bell holds the time.
Be a renunciant at home. The Tenth Guru's shabad: think of your house as the forest, stay unattached within, and wear self-control, mercy and the Name as the hermit's marks.
screen: `BE A RENUNCIANT AT HOME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the forest at home. Today, find one minute of stillness in the busiest room you're in, and keep it to yourself. Day six hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing re man aiso kar sanniaasaa in kirtan as a picture of the householder's path: detachment and devotion lived inside family and work.

it takes the forest life seriously and moves its meaning indoors.
Sikh teaching honors the householder's life

fork.setup: you want to renounce the world and find God. where does the Tenth Guru's shabad tell your mind to go?
options: to a cave in the mountains.
nowhere: think of your house as the forest, and be unattached within.
fork.reveal: the shabad keeps the renunciation but moves it home: self-control as matted hair, the Name as ashes.

original.note: Gurmukhi: renunciation; re man aiso kar sanniaasaa, O mind, renounce like this.

trapdoor: what you thought: renunciation means leaving home.
what it means: the shabad makes the house the forest and the heart the hermitage.
what a scholar hears: the Tenth Guru reinterprets the sannyasi's signs one by one, in line with the Gurus' long emphasis on the householder's path.

notes: Editor review (y2 669-687): hook no longer tells the listener 'everyone has had the fantasy'; the overbroad 'the Gurus were householders, with families, farms and work' narrowed to Guru Nanak and the householder ideal (myth item rewritten to match); added pride (hankaar) to the list of vices, as in the shabad.

Shabad paraphrased: house as forest, detached within; self-control as matted hair, union as bathing, wisdom as guru, the Name as ashes; eat and sleep little; mercy, forgiveness, contentment; free of lust, anger, greed, attachment. Confirm the item-by-item mapping.
Gloss of udaas as 'unattached, free inside': confirm.
